e: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection
d: Ethernet media access method — if the sender detects a collision, it sends a jamming signal and all nodes cease transmitting, resuming after a random time.
The first 24 bits of a MAC address, assigned to a particular manufacturer. The manufacturer then manages and assigns the remaining 24-bit vendor portion.
The model used by the CCNA 200-301 exam. The five-layer model splits Network Access into separate Physical and Data-Link layers.
The Application layer's PDU has no specific name in the TCP/IP model.

e: The set of devices that could cause a collision if they transmit at the same time
d: A hub puts all connected devices in one collision domain; each switch port is its own collision domain.

e: The set of devices that receive each other's broadcast traffic
d: Each switch port shares one broadcast domain per VLAN; each router interface is a separate broadcast domain.
Used to connect two like devices (e.g. switch-to-switch) directly. Largely obsolete now that Auto-MDIX auto-detects the correct wiring.
1000BASE-T uses all 8 pins (1-8).

t: Ethernet II frame — Preamble and SFD
e: 7-byte Preamble for synchronisation, then a 1-byte Start Frame Delimiter (SFD, aka SOF)
d: The SFD signals that the next byte begins the destination MAC address field.

e: 2 bytes; defines the type of packet carried inside the frame
d: Can be replaced by a 4-byte 802.1Q header when the frame is tagged for a VLAN.
Padded up to 46 bytes if the real payload is shorter than that.
A 4-byte checksum at the end of an Ethernet frame. The receiver discards the frame if the FCS doesn't check out.
The last 23 bits map to the relevant multicast IP address. Since multicast IPs have 28 variable bits, one multicast MAC maps to 32 possible IPs.
A point-to-point Layer 2 protocol. Its Type field is Cisco-proprietary, so HDLC reliably interoperates only between Cisco devices.
Client sends a segment with the SYN flag; server responds with SYN+ACK; client responds with ACK to establish the connection.
Host A sends ACK+FIN; Host B acknowledges then sends its own ACK+FIN; Host A responds with ACK. The RST flag can also tear down a connection abruptly.

e: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable (sequence/ack numbers, retransmission); UDP is connectionless, unreliable "best effort"
d: UDP suits real-time traffic like voice, where a retransmitted segment would arrive too late to be useful anyway.

e: The amount of data a sender will transmit before waiting for an ACK with the expected acknowledgment number
d: Set by the receiver. It grows gradually if there are no transmission problems, and shrinks if segments go missing, indicating congestion.

e: Equal to the sequence number of the next segment the receiver expects
d: If the receiver replies with an earlier acknowledgment number than expected, a segment was lost and the sender resends from that point.
Set in the SYN segment's options; equal to the outgoing link's MTU minus 20 bytes for the TCP header. MTU can be auto-discovered.
